tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The wiki (dated 2020-01-21) has raw wrk output for actix-web 2.0.0 and cpv-framework 0.2.0.0 and states the CPU (Xeon E31225 @ 3.10GHz). The code is public: benchmarks/_runner.py, benchmarks/targets/cpv-framework/Main.cpp and benchmarks/targets/actix-web/src/main.rs (both 'Hello World!' on GET /). build.sh gives g++-9 with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release and cargo build --release, so code, compiler, flags and CPU are all stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: cpv-framework 0.2.0.0 vs actix-web 2.0.0 (wrk, best of 3): 84,691.95 vs 80,516.92 req/s (1 core, 100 conns, ~1.05x); 170,555.82 vs 149,625.67 (2 cores, 100 conns, ~1.14x); 76,556.09 vs 71,222.78 (1 core, 10000 conns, ~1.07x); 72,151.32 vs 58,860.81 (1 core, 20000 conns, ~1.23x); 123,234.96 vs 61,898.53 (2 cores, 20000 conns, ~1.99x, but actix-web returned 177,988 non-2xx responses in that run); at 2 cores/10000 conns cpv-framework was slower (136,694.89 vs 141,524.73, ~0.97x). All ratios derived from page data.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: cpv-framework: g++-9, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG), C++17, -Wall -Wextra plus Seastar pkg-config CFLAGS; run with --smp=$(nproc) --task-quota-ms=20 --reactor-backend=epoll. actix-web: cargo build --release (rustc version not stated).
corrections.workload: 'Hello World!' plaintext response on GET /, wrk (throughput) and wrk2 (fixed-rate latency), 60-180 s runs, best of 3; server pinned to 1 or 2 cores and client to cores 2,3 via taskset; 100, 10000 and 20000 connections; Intel Xeon E31225 @ 3.10GHz (4 cores).
corrections.caveats: First-party wiki benchmark from January 2020 against actix-web 2.0.0 (several major versions old); the project has had no commits since 2020-01-21. cpv-framework loses to actix-web at 2 cores/10000 connections. It also loses to plain seastar-httpd (the framework it is built on) in every throughput configuration on the same page (e.g. 184,507 vs 170,556 req/s at 2 cores/100 conns). actix-web's 20000-connection results include many non-2xx responses, so the ~1.2-2x gaps there are not clean. rustc version and Seastar's exact CFLAGS are not stated.

notes: Wiki numbers match the record apart from the 1-core/10000-connection ratio (1.07x, not 1.08x). Tier upgraded to A because the in-repo build scripts give the compiler and flags, and the wiki gives the CPU model. Metadata checked: MIT, 122 stars, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2020-01-21 (abandoned).

tier_reason: The Google Sheet ('Crow benchmark result (2014. 10. 2)') has req/s for crow, netty, go, play2 and express at concurrency 16-16384. It was made by Crow's original author. The linked ipkn/crow-benchmark repo gives the code (go/src/hello/hello.go is the TechEmpower net/http code; crow is a submodule at 3e5e91c) and the instance type, but no compiler, flags or CPU model, so it stays first-party C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Crow: 136,297-296,733 req/s vs Go net/http (TechEmpower reference code): 92,893-180,517 req/s at concurrency 16-16384, i.e. ~1.46x-1.64x higher throughput at every level (e.g. 296,733 vs 180,517 at 4096, ~1.64x; lowest gap 233,349 vs 159,935 at 64, ~1.46x). Ratios derived from page data.
corrections.workload: TechEmpower '/json' test (simple JSON response {"message":"Hello, World!"}), with the Go, Netty and Play code copied from TechEmpower/FrameworkBenchmarks; wrk load generator using 8 cores; concurrency 16, 64, 256, 1024, 4096 and 16384.
corrections.hardware: AWS EC2 c3.8xlarge; wrk used 8 cores for load generation (the README does not say whether the client ran on the same instance); CPU model not stated.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark by Crow's original author (ipkn), dated 2014-10-02 in the sheet title; the benchmark repo's commits are all from 2014-09-27 to 2014-10-01. It tested the 2014 ipkn/crow code (submodule commit 3e5e91c), not current CrowCpp/Crow, and an old Go release. Results exist only in the Google Sheet and its charts. No compiler, flags or CPU model are stated. Crow is slightly behind Netty at concurrency 16384 (257,296 vs 262,335). Crow is not in the TechEmpower rounds, so there is no independent re-run. The LICENSE file is BSD-3-Clause for the code (the GitHub API reports NOASSERTION), but the Crow logo and graphics are under a separate all-rights-reserved copyright.

notes: Sheet numbers match the record's endpoints exactly. The '1.3x-1.7x' range was imprecise; the page data gives 1.46x-1.64x. Corrected workload ('/json', not plaintext) and date (2014, not ~2015-2018). Metadata checked: 4,983 stars, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-23 (active).

tier_reason: First-party page with charts against nginx: static-file req/s per core (nginx 1.9.10 vs H2O 1.7.0-beta4) and labelled download timings (nginx 1.9.5 vs H2O 1.5.0). The server configs are public (gists kazuho/969bb99bae31d67e01c4 and def1e71281ed4ae07b95; one worker each). Only the instance type (c3.8xlarge) is given, with no CPU model, compiler or build flags, so it stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Static-file chart (612-byte file, 250 clients, req/s per core; bar heights read from the chart gridlines, so approximate): nginx 1.9.10 vs H2O 1.7.0-beta4 ~74K vs ~108K (HTTP/1.1, ~1.5x), ~45K vs ~79K (HTTP/1.1 TLS, ~1.7x), ~77K vs ~340K (HTTP/2 TLS, ~4.4x). Download-timings chart (labelled values, 8Mbps/100ms, H2O 1.5.0 HTTP/2 vs nginx 1.9.5 HTTP/1.1 / HTTP/2): load 2.96 vs 3.32/3.17 s (Chrome 45), 2.74 vs 3.01/2.82 s (Firefox 41), 2.97 vs 3.28/3.06 s (Safari iOS 9.0.1); first paint 1.74 vs 2.44/3.00 s (Chrome), 1.27 vs 1.48/1.83 s (Firefox), but on Safari 2.01 s vs 1.85/2.56 s, so H2O's first paint is slower than nginx HTTP/1.1 there. Ratios derived from page data.
corrections.workload: 612-byte static file on two Amazon EC2 c3.8xlarge instances (server + client) in one placement group, 250 concurrent clients, wrk (HTTP/1) and h2load (HTTP/2), one worker per server (h2o num-threads: 1, nginx worker_processes 1), nginx open_file_cache enabled vs H2O's built-in open-file cache; plus first-paint/load times of an http2rulez.com fork in Chrome 45, Firefox 41 and Safari iOS 9.0.1 over a tc/netem-simulated 8Mbps/100ms link; plus an older reverse-proxy chart (h2o 0.9.0 vs nginx 1.7.7).
corrections.caveats: First-party page. It was last changed in 2016 (benchmark update 2016-02-04, typo fix 2016-08-23), so it compares H2O 1.5/1.7 with nginx 1.9.x; the reverse-proxy chart (h2o 0.9.0 vs nginx 1.7.7) is called 'old' on the page. Static-file values exist only as bar heights, but the download-timing chart has labelled values. Single-worker runs only, so multi-core scaling is not shown. H2O is not faster everywhere: on Safari iOS its first paint (2.01 s) is slower than nginx HTTP/1.1 (1.85 s). No CPU model, compiler or build flags are stated for either server.

notes: Downgraded because the claim was overstated. 'First-paint sooner than nginx' fails for Safari against nginx HTTP/1.1, and the record wrongly said no numbers could be read (the download chart has labels). Tier C stands. Metadata checked: MIT, 11,546 stars, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-10 (active).
